fields.Question: You moved shop.example.com to a new IP and updated the A record. The old record had a TTL of 86400. Hours later some users still hit the old server. What is the most likely cause?
fields.Choices:
DNS propagation between authoritative servers is broken
Resolvers and clients cached the old record and will keep it until the 86400 second TTL expires
Browsers ignore DNS TTLs entirely
The new A record needs a matching PTR record before it is used
fields.Correct: Resolvers and clients cached the old record and will keep it until the 86400 second TTL expires
fields.Explanation: Recursive resolvers, OS stubs and browsers may cache an answer for up to its TTL, so a one day TTL means up to a day of stale answers. Lower the TTL well before a migration. Propagation is not a push process between authoritative servers, it is cache expiry. Browsers do honor TTLs (often capping them shorter). PTR records are for reverse lookups and play no part in forward resolution.
fields.Hint: Nothing pushes DNS changes; caches just expire.
fields.Source:
RFC 1034 Domain Names, Concepts and Facilities (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1034)
ByteByteGo, What happens when you type google.com (https://bytebytego.com/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-google/)

fields.Question: A client in Sydney makes its first HTTPS request (HTTP/1.1 over TCP, TLS 1.3, DNS already cached) to a server with 150 ms RTT. Roughly how long until the first response byte arrives, ignoring server time?
fields.Choices:
450 ms
150 ms
300 ms
600 ms
fields.Correct: 450 ms
fields.Explanation: TCP handshake costs 1 RTT, the TLS 1.3 handshake 1 RTT, then the request and response 1 RTT: 3 x 150 = 450 ms. 150 ms ignores both handshakes. 300 ms forgets one of them (often candidates assume TLS is free). 600 ms is the TLS 1.2 number, which needed 2 RTTs for the full handshake.
fields.Hint: Count handshakes, then add the request itself.
fields.Source:
High Performance Browser Networking, Ilya Grigorik (https://hpbn.co/)
RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446)

fields.Question: A page loads 20 small API calls to the same origin over HTTPS. After the first call, the rest are noticeably faster even though the server time is unchanged. What explains this best?
fields.Choices:
The server JIT compiled its handlers
DNS answers are smaller after the first lookup
TCP slow start makes later connections start with a larger window
The browser reused the already established TCP and TLS connection, skipping the handshakes
fields.Correct: The browser reused the already established TCP and TLS connection, skipping the handshakes
fields.Explanation: Persistent connections (keep-alive in HTTP/1.1, multiplexing in HTTP/2) let later requests skip DNS, TCP and TLS setup, saving 1 to 2 RTTs each. Server time was stated unchanged, so JIT is ruled out. DNS answer size does not change. Slow start applies per connection; a new connection starts small again, so it argues for reuse rather than explaining new connections being faster.
fields.Hint: What did the first request pay for that the others did not?
fields.Source:
RFC 9112 HTTP/1.1 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112)
High Performance Browser Networking, Ilya Grigorik (https://hpbn.co/)

fields.Question: Users in Europe load a static JS bundle from an origin in us-east. You put a CDN in front with a long Cache-Control max-age. Why does p50 load time drop most for repeat requests from Europe?
fields.Choices:
The CDN compresses files better than the origin
CDNs use UDP so there is no handshake
The edge serves the cached file from a nearby POP, so handshakes and transfer cross a much shorter RTT
The browser stops validating the TLS certificate for CDN domains
fields.Correct: The edge serves the cached file from a nearby POP, so handshakes and transfer cross a much shorter RTT
fields.Explanation: Latency is dominated by round trips times distance. A cache hit at a nearby POP turns a transatlantic RTT of around 80 to 100 ms into a few ms for every handshake and data round trip. Compression may help but is not the main effect and origins can compress too. CDNs mostly serve HTTP over TCP and TLS; even with HTTP/3 there is still a handshake. Certificate validation is never skipped.
fields.Hint: Speed of light, not bandwidth.
fields.Source:
ByteByteGo, What happens when you type google.com (https://bytebytego.com/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-google/)
High Performance Browser Networking, Ilya Grigorik (https://hpbn.co/)

fields.Question: A user types shop.example.com (no scheme). The site sends Strict-Transport-Security on HTTPS responses and is not on the browser preload list. On the very first visit, which statement is true?
fields.Choices:
HSTS forces HTTPS on the first visit because the header is sent by DNS
The first request can go out over plain HTTP and is then redirected; HSTS only protects later visits
The browser always tries HTTPS first, so HSTS is redundant
HSTS encrypts the DNS query for the host
fields.Correct: The first request can go out over plain HTTP and is then redirected; HSTS only protects later visits
fields.Explanation: HSTS is trust on first use: the browser learns the policy from an HTTPS response, so the first plain HTTP request is exposed to downgrade attacks. Preloading closes that gap. The header is an HTTP response header, not DNS. Many browsers now try HTTPS first, but HSTS still matters because it forbids falling back and blocks click-through on certificate errors. HSTS has nothing to do with DNS encryption.
fields.Hint: Where does the browser learn the policy from?
fields.Source: RFC 6797 HTTP Strict Transport Security (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6797)

fields.Question: You create api2.example.com. A teammate queried it five minutes before you created it and got NXDOMAIN. They still get NXDOMAIN now while you resolve it fine. What governs how long their resolver keeps the NXDOMAIN?
fields.Choices:
Negative caching, bounded by the zone SOA record (minimum field and SOA TTL)
The TTL of the new A record
NXDOMAIN is never cached
The browser HSTS max-age
fields.Correct: Negative caching, bounded by the zone SOA record (minimum field and SOA TTL)
fields.Explanation: RFC 2308 lets resolvers cache NXDOMAIN for the lesser of the SOA TTL and the SOA minimum field. Their resolver has not asked again. The new A record TTL is irrelevant because their resolver never fetched that record. Saying NXDOMAIN is never cached is the common misconception that causes this confusion. HSTS concerns HTTPS policy, not DNS.
fields.Hint: Answers that say 'does not exist' are cached too.
fields.Source: RFC 2308 Negative Caching of DNS Queries (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2308)

fields.Question: You push live score updates one way, server to browser, to millions of clients. Clients never send data back on that channel, and you want automatic reconnect with resume. Which transport fits best?
fields.Choices:
WebSockets
Short polling every second
Long polling
Server-Sent Events
fields.Correct: Server-Sent Events
fields.Explanation: SSE is a one way stream over plain HTTP with built in reconnect and Last-Event-ID resume, and it works through ordinary HTTP infrastructure. WebSockets work but add a bidirectional protocol you do not need and you must build reconnect and resume yourself; picking them by default is the classic mistake. Short polling wastes requests and adds up to a second of lag. Long polling costs a new request per update and is a fallback, not the first choice.
fields.Hint: Which option has resume built into the browser API?
fields.Source:
WHATWG HTML Standard, Server-sent events (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html)
Hello Interview, Networking Essentials (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/core-concepts/networking-essentials)

fields.Question: A chat app needs low latency messages in both directions, typing indicators, and presence, on web and mobile. Which transport fits best?
fields.Choices:
Server-Sent Events plus a POST per typing keystroke
Short polling every 500 ms
WebSockets
HTTP/2 server push
fields.Correct: WebSockets
fields.Explanation: Frequent bidirectional small messages are what WebSockets are for: one long lived connection, low per message overhead. SSE plus POSTs works for occasional client sends but a POST per keystroke adds request overhead and ordering complexity. Short polling at 500 ms adds latency and load. HTTP/2 server push pushes resources into the browser cache, was never a message API, and browsers have removed it.
fields.Hint: Both directions, often, small messages.
fields.Source:
RFC 6455 The WebSocket Protocol (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455)
Hello Interview, Networking Essentials (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/core-concepts/networking-essentials)

fields.Question: Mobile clients hold a WebSocket to a notification service. Phones drop connections when switching networks. Users complain they miss notifications sent while reconnecting. What is the correct fix?
fields.Choices:
Increase the WebSocket ping interval
Give each message a per user sequence number, persist recent messages, and on reconnect the client sends its last seen sequence so the server replays the gap
Switch to TCP keepalive with a shorter timer
Send each notification twice
fields.Correct: Give each message a per user sequence number, persist recent messages, and on reconnect the client sends its last seen sequence so the server replays the gap
fields.Explanation: A connection is not a delivery guarantee. Anything sent while the socket is down is lost unless it is stored and replayed from a cursor. Ping intervals and TCP keepalive only detect dead connections faster; they cannot recover messages already lost. Sending twice still loses both copies if the client is offline for both, and creates duplicates otherwise.
fields.Hint: The socket was down; where do the messages live?
fields.Source:
Hello Interview, Networking Essentials (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/core-concepts/networking-essentials)
WHATWG HTML Standard, Server-sent events (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html)

fields.Question: Your enterprise customers sit behind proxies that break WebSocket upgrades but allow normal HTTP. You need near real time order status updates, a few per minute per user. What is the pragmatic choice?
fields.Choices:
Long polling or SSE over regular HTTP
Insist on WebSockets and ask customers to change proxies
Raw UDP from the browser
Poll every 30 seconds
fields.Correct: Long polling or SSE over regular HTTP
fields.Explanation: Both run over standard HTTP requests and responses, so they pass through proxies that drop Upgrade, and a few updates per minute is well within their cost. Telling customers to fix their network is not a design answer. Browsers cannot open raw UDP sockets. Polling every 30 seconds misses the near real time requirement.
fields.Hint: What survives a proxy that only understands plain HTTP?
fields.Source: Hello Interview, Networking Essentials (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/core-concepts/networking-essentials)

fields.Question: A WebSocket gateway fleet of 50 nodes holds user connections. A message for user U can be produced by any backend service. How should a producer reach the node that holds U's socket?
fields.Choices:
Broadcast every message to all 50 nodes over HTTP
Use sticky sessions on the producer side
Store messages in the gateway's local memory and let the client poll
Keep a connection registry (user to gateway node) or use a pub/sub channel per user or shard that the owning gateway subscribes to
fields.Correct: Keep a connection registry (user to gateway node) or use a pub/sub channel per user or shard that the owning gateway subscribes to
fields.Explanation: The gateway that owns the socket must be found by lookup or subscription; that decouples producers from where users are connected. Broadcasting to all nodes makes every node do 50x work and does not scale. Sticky sessions pin a client to a backend, they do nothing for a producer that is a different service. Local memory plus polling throws away the point of a push channel.
fields.Hint: Producers do not know where the socket is.
fields.Source: Hello Interview, Networking Essentials (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/core-concepts/networking-essentials)

fields.Question: A dashboard polls GET /status every 2 seconds. 100,000 users keep it open, and status changes about once a minute. What is the main problem with this design?
fields.Choices:
Polling cannot work through load balancers
HTTP GET cannot be cached
About 50,000 requests per second, almost all returning unchanged data
Polling requires WebSocket support on the server
fields.Correct: About 50,000 requests per second, almost all returning unchanged data
fields.Explanation: 100,000 / 2 s = 50,000 rps, and with one change per minute around 97 percent of responses are wasted. Long polling, SSE or conditional requests fix that. Polling is plain HTTP and works fine through load balancers. GET responses can be cached and conditional (ETag), which helps but does not remove the request rate. Polling needs nothing beyond HTTP.
fields.Hint: Do the arithmetic.
fields.Source: Hello Interview, Networking Essentials (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/core-concepts/networking-essentials)

fields.Question: Design the delivery path for real time in app notifications for 10 million daily users across web and mobile. Talk through transport, connection routing, missed messages and scale.
fields.Answer:
Transport: SSE for web if it is one way, WebSockets if the app already needs client sends; mobile uses the socket while foregrounded and APNs or FCM push when backgrounded.

Routing: gateway fleet holds connections; a registry or pub/sub keyed by user lets producers reach the owning node. Gateways are mostly stateless besides the sockets.

Missed messages: persist notifications with a per user sequence; client reconnects with last seen id and the server replays. Dedup on the client by id.

Scale: estimate concurrent connections (say 20 to 30 percent of DAU), memory per connection, use L4 or connection aware balancing, drain gateways on deploy with jittered client reconnect to avoid a thundering herd.

Follow ups: ordering, fan out for group notifications, read receipts, rate limiting noisy producers.
fields.Hint: Transport, routing, replay, then capacity.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview, Networking Essentials (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/core-concepts/networking-essentials)
WHATWG HTML Standard, Server-sent events (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html)

fields.Question: Chat clients hold WebSockets behind an L7 load balancer using round robin. After a rolling deploy, the first nodes to come back hold most connections while the newest nodes sit nearly idle. What actually fixes the imbalance?
fields.Choices:
Balance on active connections (least connections) and have overloaded nodes gradually shed connections so clients reconnect with jitter
Enable sticky sessions
Switch the LB to L4
Increase the health check interval
fields.Correct: Balance on active connections (least connections) and have overloaded nodes gradually shed connections so clients reconnect with jitter
fields.Explanation: Round robin balances new connections, not existing ones, and long lived sockets never move on their own. Least connections steers new ones to idle nodes and controlled shedding redistributes the old ones. Sticky sessions make it worse by pinning clients to where they already are; it is the common wrong full fix. L4 versus L7 does not change that connections are long lived. Health check intervals affect failure detection, not distribution.
fields.Hint: Long lived connections never get rebalanced by themselves.
fields.Source:
Envoy docs, Load balancing (https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/load_balancing)
Crack the Offer, System Design Load Balancing (https://www.cracktheoffer.com/system-design-load-balancing)

fields.Question: You need to route /api/* to one service and /images/* to another, and add a header with the client's request id. Which load balancer type is required?
fields.Choices:
L4 (TCP) load balancer
DNS round robin
Anycast
L7 (HTTP) load balancer
fields.Correct: L7 (HTTP) load balancer
fields.Explanation: Path routing and header rewriting need the balancer to parse HTTP, which is L7. An L4 balancer forwards TCP or UDP flows by address and port and never sees the path. DNS round robin only picks an IP per lookup. Anycast routes packets to the nearest site and knows nothing about HTTP.
fields.Hint: Who can read the URL path?
fields.Source:
AWS Elastic Load Balancing, How it works (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/userguide/how-elastic-load-balancing-works.html)
Crack the Offer, System Design Load Balancing (https://www.cracktheoffer.com/system-design-load-balancing)

fields.Question: A legacy app stores sessions in process memory, so the team enables cookie based sticky sessions. Which problem does this introduce?
fields.Choices:
Requests can no longer be encrypted with TLS
Sticky sessions require L4 load balancing
Load skews toward nodes with heavy users, and when a node dies or is drained its users lose their sessions
Sticky sessions double request latency
fields.Correct: Load skews toward nodes with heavy users, and when a node dies or is drained its users lose their sessions
fields.Explanation: Affinity trades even balancing for locality: hot users pile on one node, autoscaling helps only new users, and a node failure takes its sessions with it. The usual fix is an external session store. TLS still works, the L7 balancer terminates it to read the cookie. Cookie stickiness actually requires L7, not L4. It adds no meaningful latency.
fields.Hint: What happens to the session when the node goes away?
fields.Source:
AWS Elastic Load Balancing, How it works (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/userguide/how-elastic-load-balancing-works.html)
Crack the Offer, System Design Load Balancing (https://www.cracktheoffer.com/system-design-load-balancing)

fields.Question: Your LB health check hits /health, which queries the shared database. The database has a 10 second slowdown and every app node fails its check at once. What is the problem with this design?
fields.Choices:
Health checks should use UDP
A deep check tied to a shared dependency can mark the whole fleet unhealthy at once, so the LB has nowhere to send traffic
The check interval should be 1 ms
Health checks should run only at deploy time
fields.Correct: A deep check tied to a shared dependency can mark the whole fleet unhealthy at once, so the LB has nowhere to send traffic
fields.Explanation: Liveness checks for load balancing should reflect whether this node can serve, not whether a shared dependency is slow, otherwise a dependency blip removes every node and turns a partial outage into a total one. Many LBs fail open when all targets are unhealthy, but you should not rely on it. Transport protocol is irrelevant. A 1 ms interval only adds load. Checks must run continuously to catch node failures.
fields.Hint: If every node depends on it, every node fails together.
fields.Source:
AWS Elastic Load Balancing, How it works (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/userguide/how-elastic-load-balancing-works.html)
Google SRE Book, Addressing Cascading Failures (https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)

fields.Question: Requests to a service vary wildly in cost: most take 5 ms but some take 2 s. With plain round robin, some backends build long queues while others are idle. Which algorithm usually helps most?
fields.Choices:
Least outstanding requests (or power of two choices on active requests)
Random
IP hash
Weighted round robin with equal weights
fields.Correct: Least outstanding requests (or power of two choices on active requests)
fields.Explanation: Picking the backend with fewer in flight requests reacts to actual load, so slow requests do not stack up on one node. Random has the same blindness as round robin. IP hash pins clients to backends and ignores load. Weighted round robin with equal weights is just round robin.
fields.Hint: Pick based on what the backend is doing right now.
fields.Source: Envoy docs, Load balancing (https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/load_balancing)

fields.Question: Behind an L7 load balancer, your app logs every request as coming from 10.0.3.7, the LB's address. How do you get the real client IP?
fields.Choices:
Read the TCP source address more carefully
Ask the client to send its IP in the body
Switch DNS to round robin
Read X-Forwarded-For (or Forwarded) set by the LB, trusting only the entry your own LB appended
fields.Correct: Read X-Forwarded-For (or Forwarded) set by the LB, trusting only the entry your own LB appended
fields.Explanation: An L7 proxy opens its own connection to the app, so the TCP source is the proxy. It records the client in X-Forwarded-For or Forwarded. Clients can spoof earlier entries, so trust only what your proxy added. The TCP source address is accurate, it is just the LB. A client sent IP is untrustworthy and often a private NAT address. DNS changes nothing here.
fields.Hint: The LB opened a new connection.
fields.Source:
AWS Elastic Load Balancing, How it works (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/userguide/how-elastic-load-balancing-works.html)
RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)

fields.Question: A client retries every 100 ms on 503 from a struggling service. Thousands of clients do the same. What is the correct client behavior?
fields.Choices:
Retry immediately since GET is idempotent
Retry on a fixed 1 second interval forever
Exponential backoff with jitter, honor Retry-After, and cap retries with a retry budget
Never retry any error
fields.Correct: Exponential backoff with jitter, honor Retry-After, and cap retries with a retry budget
fields.Explanation: 503 means the server is overloaded or down; synchronized fast retries multiply load and keep it down. Backoff spreads retries over time, jitter breaks synchronization, a budget caps the total extra load. Idempotency makes a retry safe, not cheap. A fixed interval still synchronizes clients and never stops. Never retrying gives up on transient failures that a retry would fix.
fields.Hint: Safe to retry is not the same as good to retry now.
fields.Source:
AWS Architecture Blog, Exponential Backoff and Jitter (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/)
Amazon Builders' Library, Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)

fields.Question: Your API rejects a client because it exceeded its rate limit. Which response is correct?
fields.Choices:
500 Internal Server Error
429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header
503 Service Unavailable with no headers
400 Bad Request
fields.Correct: 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header
fields.Explanation: 429 says the client sent too many requests and Retry-After tells it when to come back. 500 claims a server bug, which pages your on call and makes clients retry blindly. 503 signals the whole service is unavailable, not this client's quota. 400 says the request itself is malformed, which it is not.
fields.Hint: Whose fault is it, and when can they try again?
fields.Source:
RFC 6585 Additional HTTP Status Codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585)
PracHub, Cloudflare Software Engineer Interview Questions Guide (https://prachub.com/interview-guide/cloudflare-software-engineer-interview-questions-guide-2026)

fields.Question: A payment POST times out on the client. The client does not know if the charge happened. How do you make the retry safe?
fields.Choices:
Send a client generated idempotency key; the server stores the result per key and returns the stored result on a repeat
Retry with PUT instead of POST
Retry only after 24 hours
Have the client check its logs first
fields.Correct: Send a client generated idempotency key; the server stores the result per key and returns the stored result on a repeat
fields.Explanation: A timeout is ambiguous: the request may have succeeded. An idempotency key lets the server detect the duplicate and replay the original outcome instead of charging twice. Switching verbs does not make the server logic idempotent. Waiting does not resolve the ambiguity. The client logs only show that the response never arrived.
fields.Hint: A timeout does not mean it failed.
fields.Source: Stripe API docs, Idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)

fields.Question: A request flows through 4 service layers. Each layer retries a failing call to the layer below up to 3 times (4 attempts total). The bottom service is down. How many attempts can hit the bottom service for one user request?
fields.Explanation: Retries multiply across layers: 4 attempts at each of 4 layers gives 4^4 = 256 attempts on the bottom service. This is how retry storms keep an outage going. The fix is retrying at one layer only (usually the edge or the caller nearest the failure) plus retry budgets. 4 counts a single layer. 12 adds instead of multiplying. 16 covers only two layers.
fields.Hint: Each attempt above triggers a full set below.
fields.Source:
Amazon Builders' Library, Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)
Google SRE Book, Addressing Cascading Failures (https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)

fields.Question: The edge has a 2 s timeout for a user request. It calls service A, which calls B with its own default 30 s timeout. B hangs. What goes wrong and what is the fix?
fields.Choices:
Nothing, the edge timeout protects everything
B should have a longer timeout
A keeps waiting on B for 30 s after the user is gone, tying up threads and connections; propagate a deadline so each hop uses the remaining budget
Set every timeout to 30 s for consistency
fields.Correct: A keeps waiting on B for 30 s after the user is gone, tying up threads and connections; propagate a deadline so each hop uses the remaining budget
fields.Explanation: Timeouts must shrink as you go deeper. Without deadline propagation, work continues long after the caller gave up, and a hanging dependency exhausts A's resources, cascading upward. The edge timeout only frees the edge. Longer timeouts make the pile up worse. Uniform 30 s timeouts ignore that the user budget is 2 s.
fields.Hint: Who is still waiting after the user leaves?
fields.Source:
Amazon Builders' Library, Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)
Google SRE Book, Addressing Cascading Failures (https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)

fields.Question: Your load balancer returns errors. In case one, no healthy backend exists. In case two, a backend accepted the request but did not respond in time. Which pair of codes is correct?
fields.Choices:
502 then 500
503 then 504
504 then 503
500 then 502
fields.Correct: 503 then 504
fields.Explanation: 503 Service Unavailable means the server or gateway cannot handle it now, which is what an LB returns with no healthy targets. 504 Gateway Timeout means the upstream did not answer in time. 502 means the upstream sent an invalid response or reset the connection. 500 is a generic error in the server itself. Swapping 503 and 504 is the common slip.
fields.Hint: One is about availability, the other about waiting.
fields.Source:
RFC 9110 HTTP Semantics (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)
AWS Elastic Load Balancing, How it works (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/userguide/how-elastic-load-balancing-works.html)

fields.Question: New York to Sydney is about 16,000 km. Light in fiber travels roughly 200,000 km/s. What is the best possible RTT, ignoring routing detours and processing?
fields.Choices:
About 160 ms
About 40 ms
About 80 ms
About 320 ms
fields.Correct: About 160 ms
fields.Explanation: One way is 16,000 / 200,000 = 80 ms, so a round trip is at least 160 ms. Real RTTs are higher because cables do not follow great circles. 80 ms is the one way figure, the most common mistake. 40 ms would need faster than light. 320 ms double counts the round trip.
fields.Hint: Round trip means there and back.
fields.Source: High Performance Browser Networking, Ilya Grigorik (https://hpbn.co/)

fields.Question: An app server is in us-east. A user in Singapore (RTT 230 ms) loads a page that makes 3 sequential API calls, each needing one round trip on an already warm connection. The product team wants under 300 ms. What is the effective fix?
fields.Choices:
Buy more bandwidth for the user
Use a faster JSON library
Enable gzip
Serve from a region near Singapore (or collapse the 3 calls into one and cache at the edge), because 3 x 230 ms is already 690 ms of pure RTT
fields.Correct: Serve from a region near Singapore (or collapse the 3 calls into one and cache at the edge), because 3 x 230 ms is already 690 ms of pure RTT
fields.Explanation: Sequential round trips over a long RTT dominate; only fewer round trips or a shorter distance helps. Bandwidth does not reduce RTT for small requests. Faster serialization saves microseconds to milliseconds. Gzip shrinks bytes but small API responses already fit in a few packets.
fields.Hint: Latency, not bandwidth.
fields.Source:
High Performance Browser Networking, Ilya Grigorik (https://hpbn.co/)
Hello Interview, Networking Essentials (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/core-concepts/networking-essentials)

fields.Question: Mobile users reconnect often and each new connection costs TCP plus TLS handshakes on a 200 ms RTT. Which change cuts the most connection setup time for returning clients?
fields.Choices:
Increase the certificate key size
Turn off TCP Nagle
Use TLS 1.3 session resumption, optionally with 0-RTT for idempotent requests, or HTTP/3 which combines transport and TLS setup
Shorten the DNS TTL
fields.Correct: Use TLS 1.3 session resumption, optionally with 0-RTT for idempotent requests, or HTTP/3 which combines transport and TLS setup
fields.Explanation: Resumption skips certificate work and 0-RTT lets data go with the first flight; QUIC merges the transport and crypto handshakes into 1 RTT. 0-RTT data can be replayed, so it is only for idempotent requests. Larger keys make the handshake slower. Nagle affects small writes on an open connection, not setup. A shorter TTL causes more DNS lookups, not fewer.
fields.Hint: Remember the previous session.
fields.Source:
RFC 8446 TLS 1.3 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446)
RFC 9000 QUIC (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)

fields.Question: An interviewer asks: a page in Mumbai takes 1.8 s to first byte from your us-west origin. Break down where that time likely goes and what you would change first.
fields.Answer:
Start with RTT (around 250 ms Mumbai to us-west). Cold path: DNS (maybe 1 RTT to a resolver plus authoritative), TCP 1 RTT, TLS 1 RTT, request 1 RTT, so roughly 1 s before server time. Add redirects (http to https, apex to www) at 1 RTT each, and slow server or DB work.

Fixes in order: CDN or edge termination near users (handshakes become local), remove redirects, connection reuse, TLS 1.3 or HTTP/3, then a regional deploy or edge cache for dynamic parts. Measure with timing breakdowns (curl -w or browser timing) before guessing.
fields.Hint: Count round trips times RTT before touching the server.
fields.Source:
High Performance Browser Networking, Ilya Grigorik (https://hpbn.co/)
ByteByteGo, What happens when you type google.com (https://bytebytego.com/guides/what-happens-when-you-type-google/)

fields.Question: A service creates a new HTTP client per outbound request to one downstream host. Under load, calls fail with 'cannot assign requested address' while CPU sits at 20 percent. What is the fix?
fields.Choices:
Reuse a shared client with a pooled keep-alive connection set, so you stop burning ephemeral ports that sit in TIME_WAIT
Raise the thread count
Increase the downstream timeout
Add more memory
fields.Correct: Reuse a shared client with a pooled keep-alive connection set, so you stop burning ephemeral ports that sit in TIME_WAIT
fields.Explanation: Each short lived connection to the same destination uses an ephemeral port that stays in TIME_WAIT on the side that closed first (typically around 60 s on Linux), so a high request rate exhausts the port range. Reusing connections removes the churn. More threads create even more connections. Timeouts do not free ports in TIME_WAIT. Memory is not the bottleneck.
fields.Hint: Each new connection eats a port for a while after it closes.
fields.Source:
Michal Drozd, TCP TIME_WAIT and port exhaustion (https://www.michal-drozd.com/en/blog/tcp-time-wait-port-exhaustion/)
Linux tcp(7) manual (https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/tcp.7.html)

fields.Question: A service's p50 to the database is 3 ms but p99 jumps to 400 ms during peaks. Database query time p99 stays at 5 ms. The connection pool max is 10 and 200 request threads share it. What is the most likely cause?
fields.Choices:
The database is slow
DNS lookups on every query
TCP slow start on each query
Requests wait in the pool queue for a free connection; the tail is pool wait time, not query time
fields.Correct: Requests wait in the pool queue for a free connection; the tail is pool wait time, not query time
fields.Explanation: When concurrency exceeds pool size, requests queue for a connection, and that wait shows up only in the tail. Measure pool acquire time; size the pool from concurrency and query time (Little's law), within what the database can handle. The database is ruled out by its own 5 ms p99. Pooled connections do not do DNS per query. Slow start affects new connections, and a pool reuses them.
fields.Hint: The database says it is fast. Where else can time hide?
fields.Source: Dean and Barroso, The Tail at Scale (CACM 2013) (https://cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/)

fields.Question: Which side of a TCP connection ends up in TIME_WAIT?
fields.Choices:
Always the server
Always the client
The side that sends the first FIN (the active closer)
Neither, TIME_WAIT is only used for UDP
fields.Correct: The side that sends the first FIN (the active closer)
fields.Explanation: TIME_WAIT belongs to the active closer and lasts 2 x MSL to absorb delayed segments and ensure the final ACK. That is why servers that close connections themselves can accumulate TIME_WAIT sockets, and clients that close accumulate them on their side. It is not fixed to client or server. UDP has no connection state at all.
fields.Hint: Who said goodbye first?
fields.Source: RFC 9293 Transmission Control Protocol (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293)

fields.Question: A service handles 1,000 requests per second; each request holds a DB connection for 20 ms. Roughly how many connections are busy on average?
fields.Explanation: Little's law: concurrency = arrival rate x time in system = 1,000 x 0.02 s = 20. Size the pool above that for bursts, not to the request rate. 2 slips a decimal. 200 is 10x too high and can overload the database. 1,000 confuses throughput with concurrency.
fields.Hint: Rate times duration.
fields.Source: Dean and Barroso, The Tail at Scale (CACM 2013) (https://cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/)

fields.Question: A multiplayer game sends player positions 30 times a second. Why do many games use UDP (or QUIC datagrams) instead of TCP for this?
fields.Choices:
TCP head of line blocking would hold new positions behind a lost old one; with UDP the game drops stale updates and uses the latest
UDP packets travel faster through the network
UDP is encrypted by default
TCP cannot send small packets
fields.Correct: TCP head of line blocking would hold new positions behind a lost old one; with UDP the game drops stale updates and uses the latest
fields.Explanation: TCP delivers bytes in order, so one lost segment stalls everything after it until retransmission, and a retransmitted old position is useless. UDP lets the app skip it. UDP packets do not travel faster on the wire; the 'faster' claim is the common wrong answer. UDP has no encryption. TCP can send small segments fine.
fields.Hint: Is the old position worth waiting for?
fields.Source:
RFC 8085 UDP Usage Guidelines (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8085)
RFC 9293 Transmission Control Protocol (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293)

fields.Question: HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection. On a lossy mobile network, one lost packet stalls all streams. What does HTTP/3 over QUIC change?
fields.Choices:
It removes encryption to save time
It uses multiple TCP connections
It disables congestion control
Streams are independent at the transport layer, so a loss stalls only the affected stream, and connection setup combines transport and TLS
fields.Correct: Streams are independent at the transport layer, so a loss stalls only the affected stream, and connection setup combines transport and TLS
fields.Explanation: QUIC runs over UDP and does its own per stream reliable delivery, removing TCP level head of line blocking, and integrates TLS 1.3 into its 1 RTT handshake. QUIC is always encrypted. HTTP/3 uses one QUIC connection, not many TCP connections. QUIC has congestion control like TCP.
fields.Hint: Where did the head of line blocking come from?
fields.Source: RFC 9000 QUIC (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000)
